title: The house filled with the odor (John 12:1–8)
hook: Mary of Bethany anoints his feet with costly nard

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha on the road: anastasis. Your line was love with nowhere to go. Whose name did you remember? Day five hundred fourteen.

A scent doesn't stay politely in one corner. It fills a room, gets into curtains, follows people home on their clothes. Long after the guests have gone, a house can still smell of the dinner. Six days before the Passover, Jesus is back in Bethany at a dinner, and Lazarus, the man who was dead, is sitting at the table. Then his sister Mary opens a jar, and nobody in the house can miss what happens next.
screen: `A SCENT WON'T STAY PUT.` → `SIX DAYS BEFORE THE PASCH.` → `DINNER IN BETHANY.`

segments.voice: Martha is serving. Lazarus is at the table. And Mary takes a pound of ointment, spikenard, of great price, John says. She pours it on Jesus's feet and wipes them with her hair. Then John adds one sentence that's pure memory, as if he can still smell it. The Douay-Rheims says: "and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Odour is the British spelling of odor, and here it just means scent, fragrance. Judas objects. Why wasn't this sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor? A penny there is a denarius, roughly a day's pay for a laborer, so this jar is worth three hundred days of a laborer's pay, poured out in a minute. John says plainly that Judas didn't care about the poor; he kept the purse and helped himself. Jesus defends her: let her alone, she has kept it for the day of my burial. Then: "For the poor you have always with you; but me you have not always." People sometimes hear that as a shrug about poverty. Readers who know Deuteronomy hear an echo instead: the poor will not be wanting in the land, it says, and so open your hand to them. Read that way, Jesus is saying, this moment won't come again. Mary seems to understand what the others don't: he is about to die. So she does something extravagant, physical and unforgettable. And the whole house knew.
screen: `MARTHA SERVES, LAZARUS EATS.` · `A POUND OF NARD, POURED.` · `THREE HUNDRED PENCE, AND JUDAS.` · `KEPT FOR MY BURIAL.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE FILLED WITH THE ODOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan something fragrant for someone. Sit, and breathe slowly through your nose a few times. Notice what you can smell right now, even faintly. Then think of one person and one generous thing you could do for them today that they'd notice: flowers on a table, bread warming, a candle lit before they come home, a handwritten note. Let the plan become concrete. If you pray, you can offer it the way Mary offered the jar. If you don't, just hold the person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Nard. The costly perfume Mary of Bethany poured on Jesus's feet, filling the whole house with its fragrance. Today's word.
Your line: the whole house knew. Today, do your fragrant thing, and don't apologize for how generous it is. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany at Mass on the Monday of Holy Week.

notes: Spikenard from Nardostachys jatamansi, native to the Himalayas. Confirm.
Three hundred pence as close to a year's wages (denarius as a day's pay, Matthew 20:2). Confirm framing.
John 12:1–11 as the Gospel of Monday of Holy Week. Confirm.
Western tradition at times identified Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene; deliberately not raised here. Keeper may wish to add a note.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they remember; cut the Himalayan origin of nard and 'a year's wages' (not in the cited text; now 'three hundred days of a laborer's pay' from 12:5 and Matthew 20:2); 'odour is the old spelling' corrected to British spelling; the Deuteronomy reading attributed to readers; 'Of course she is' (a jab at Martha) cut; howItsDone's July 29 line dropped (repeated day 513).
